claim: SARS-CoV-2 causes widespread damage in the lungs in the setting of an overzealous immune response.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, causes widespread damage in the lungs in the setting of an overzealous immune response whose origin remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about COVID-19 pathology.

claim: The origin of the overzealous immune response in COVID-19 remains unclear.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, causes widespread damage in the lungs in the setting of an overzealous immune response whose origin remains unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Adult lung organoids (ALOs) can be derived from adult stem cells and are scalable, propagable, personalized, and cost-effective.
source: We present a scalable, propagable, personalized, cost-effective adult stem cell-derived human lung organoid model that is complete with both proximal and distal airway epithelia.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section of the abstract describing the model characteristics.

claim: Adult lung organoids contain both proximal and distal airway epithelia.
source: We present a scalable, propagable, personalized, cost-effective adult stem cell-derived human lung organoid model that is complete with both proximal and distal airway epithelia.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a key feature of the model in the abstract.

claim: Infected ALO monolayers best recapitulated the transcriptomic signatures in diverse cohorts of COVID-19 patient-derived respiratory samples.
source: Infected ALO monolayers best recapitulated the transcriptomic signatures in diverse cohorts of COVID-19 patient-derived respiratory samples.
evidence: This is stated as a key result in the abstract.

claim: Airway (proximal) cells are critical for sustained viral infection in COVID-19.
source: The airway (proximal) cells were critical for sustained viral infection, whereas distal alveolar differentiation (AT2→AT1) was critical for mounting the overzealous host immune response in fatal disease; ALO monolayers with well-mixed proximodistal airway components recapitulated both.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: Distal alveolar differentiation (AT2→AT1) is critical for mounting the overzealous host immune response in fatal COVID-19 disease.
source: The airway (proximal) cells were critical for sustained viral infection, whereas distal alveolar differentiation (AT2→AT1) was critical for mounting the overzealous host immune response in fatal disease; ALO monolayers with well-mixed proximodistal airway components recapitulated both.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: ALO monolayers with well-mixed proximodistal airway components recapitulate both sustained viral infection and overzealous host immune response.
source: The airway (proximal) cells were critical for sustained viral infection, whereas distal alveolar differentiation (AT2→AT1) was critical for mounting the overzealous host immune response in fatal disease; ALO monolayers with well-mixed proximodistal airway components recapitulated both.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 causes diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) in the lungs.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, causes widespread inflammation and injury in the lungs, giving rise to diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) (Andrea Valeria Arrossi and Farver, 2020; Damiani et al., 2021; Borczuk et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Roden, 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: DAD in COVID-19 features marked infection and viral burden leading to apoptosis of alveolar pneumocytes.
source: diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) (Andrea Valeria Arrossi and Farver, 2020; Damiani et al., 2021; Borczuk et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Roden, 2020), featuring marked infection and viral burden leading to apoptosis of alveolar pneumocytes (Hussman, 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: DAD in COVID-19 is associated with pulmonary edema.
source: diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) (Andrea Valeria Arrossi and Farver, 2020; Damiani et al., 2021; Borczuk et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Roden, 2020), featuring marked infection and viral burden leading to apoptosis of alveolar pneumocytes (Hussman, 2020), along with pulmonary edema (Bratic and Larsson, 2013; Carsana et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: DAD leads to poor gas exchange and respiratory failure in COVID-19.
source: DAD leads to poor gas exchange and, ultimately, respiratory failure; the latter appears to be the final common mechanism of death in most patients with severe COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of DAD.

claim: Respiratory failure is the final common mechanism of death in most patients with severe COVID-19 infection.
source: DAD leads to poor gas exchange and, ultimately, respiratory failure; the latter appears to be the final common mechanism of death in most patients with severe COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion about COVID-19 mortality.

claim: A cytokine storm has been implicated in many of the deaths from COVID-19.
source: A particular challenge is to understand the out-of-control immune reaction to the SARS-CoV-2 infection known as a cytokine storm, which has been implicated in many of the deaths from COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a known aspect of COVID-19 pathology.

claim: Many rapidly developed preclinical animal models failed to develop severe clinical symptoms of COVID-19.
source: Although rapidly developed preclinical animal models have recapitulated some of the pathognomonic aspects of infection, for example, induction of disease, and transmission, and even viral shedding in the upper and lower respiratory tract, many failed to develop severe clinical symptoms (Lakdawala and Menachery, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: The need for preclinical models of COVID-19 remains both urgent and unmet.
source: Thus, the need for preclinical models remains both urgent and unmet.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion about the state of COVID-19 research.

claim: Most existing lung models do not recapitulate the heterogeneous epithelial cellularity of both proximal and distal airways.
source: While a head-to-head comparison of the key characteristics of each model can be found in Table 1, what is particularly noteworthy is that most of the models do not recapitulate the heterogeneous epithelial cellularity of both proximal and distal airways, that is, airway epithelia, basal cells, secretory club cells, and alveolar pneumocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation about existing models.

claim: iPSC-derived AT2 cells can be differentiated into proximal and distal cell types, including AT1, ciliated, and club cells.
source: Although induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived AT2 cells be differentiated into proximal and distal cell types, including AT1, ciliated, and club cells (Kawakita et al., 2020; Dye et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: iPSC-derived models lack propagability and cannot be reproducibly generated for biobanking.
source: these iPSC-derived models lack propagability and cannot be reproducibly generated for biobanking; nor can they be scaled up in cost-effective ways for use in drug screens.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of iPSC-derived models.

claim: iPSC-derived models cannot be scaled up in cost-effective ways for use in drug screens.
source: these iPSC-derived models lack propagability and cannot be reproducibly generated for biobanking; nor can they be scaled up in cost-effective ways for use in drug screens.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of iPSC-derived models.

claim: Adult lung organoid models that are complete with proximo-distal epithelia and can be grown in a sustainable mode are yet to emerge.
source: More specifically, adult lung organoid models that can be grown in a sustainable mode and are complete with proximo-distal epithelia are yet to emerge.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in the field.

claim: ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are the primary sites of entry for SARS-CoV-2.
source: To determine which cell types in the lungs might be most readily infected, we began by analyzing a human lung single-cell sequencing dataset (GSE132914) for the levels of expression of angiotensin-converting enzyme II (ACE2) and transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2), the two receptors that have been shown to be the primary sites of entry for the SARS-CoV-2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Alveolar epithelial type 2 (AT2), ciliated and club cells have the highest expression of both ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors.
source: Alveolar epithelial type 2 (AT2), ciliated and club cells emerged as the cells with the highest expression of both receptors (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: ACE2 is expressed highest in AT2 and ciliated cells.
source: These observations are consistent with published studies demonstrating that ACE2 is indeed expressed highest in AT2 and ciliated cells (Mulay et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020; Jia et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: In deceased COVID-19 patients, gas-exchanging flattened AT1 pneumocytes are virtually replaced by cuboidal AT2-like cells.
source: In a cohort of deceased COVID-19 patients, we observed by H&E (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) that gas-exchanging flattened AT1 pneumocytes are virtually replaced by cuboidal cells that were subsequently confirmed to be AT2-like cells via immunofluorescent staining with the AT2-specific marker, surfactant protein C (SFTPC; Figure 1B, upper panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, top).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Club cells express ACE2.
source: We also confirmed that club cells express ACE2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, bottom)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is present in alveolar pneumocytes of deceased COVID-19 patients.
source: When we analyzed the lungs of deceased COVID-19 patients, the presence of SARS-COV-2 in alveolar pneumocytes was also confirmed, as determined by the colocalization of viral nucleocapsid protein with SFTPC (Figure 1B, lower panel, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 virus is present in alveolar pneumocytes and in alveolar immune cells.
source: Immunohistochemistry studies further showed the presence of SARS-COV-2 virus in alveolar pneumocytes and in alveolar immune cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Alveolar pneumocytes support the interaction between epithelial cells and inflammatory cells recruited to the lung.
source: These findings are consistent with the gathering consensus that alveolar pneumocytes support the interaction between the epithelial cells and inflammatory cells recruited to the lung
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as consistent with existing knowledge.

claim: Alveolar pneumocytes contribute to the development of acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in COVID-19.
source: via mechanisms that remain unclear, they are generally believed to contribute to the development of acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), the severe hypoxemic respiratory failure during COVID-19 (Hou et al., 2020; Spagnolo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infectivity in patient-derived airway cells is highest in the proximal airway epithelium compared to the distal alveolar pneumocytes (AT1 and AT2).
source: Because prior work has demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 infectivity in patient-derived airway cells is highest in the proximal airway epithelium compared to the distal alveolar pneumocytes (AT1 and AT2) (Hou et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: AT2 pneumocytes harbor the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
source: and yet, it is the AT2 pneumocytes that harbor the virus
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation.

claim: AT1 pneumocytes are ultimately destroyed during diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) in COVID-19.
source: and the AT1 pneumocytes that are ultimately destroyed during DAD
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation.

claim: Both proximal airway and distal (alveolar pneumocyte) components play distinct roles in mounting viral infectivity and host immune response phases in COVID-19.
source: we hypothesized that both proximal airway and distal (alveolar pneumocyte) components might play distinct roles in the respiratory system to mount the so-called viral infectivity and host immune response phases of the clinical symptoms observed in COVID-19 (Chen and Li, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis with a citation.

claim: Three lung organoid lines (ALO1-3) were developed from deep lung biopsies obtained from normal regions of lung lobes surgically resected for lung cancer.
source: Three lung organoid lines were developed from deep lung biopsies obtained from the normal regions of lung lobes surgically resected for lung cancer; both genders, smokers and non-smokers, were represented (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure and table.

claim: Lung organoid expansion media that included conditioned media from L-WRN cells emerged as superior compared to alveolosphere media-I and II.
source: A growth condition that included conditioned media from L-WRN cells that express Wnt3, R-spondin, and Noggin, supplemented with recombinant growth factors, which we named as 'lung organoid expansion media,' emerged as superior compared to alveolosphere media-I and II (Jacob et al., 2019; Yamamoto et al., 2017) (details in Materials and methods), based on its ability to consistently and reproducibly support the best morphology and growth characteristics across multiple attempts to isolate organoids from lung tissue samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Three adult lung organoid lines (ALO1-3) were cultured with similar phenotypes until P10 and beyond.
source: Three adult lung organoid lines (ALO1-3) were developed using the expansion media, monitored for their growth characteristics by brightfield microscopy and cultured with similar phenotypes until P10 and beyond (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: All three ALO lines had a comparable level of AT2 cell surfactant markers compared against hiPSC-derived AT2 cells.
source: All three ALO lines had a comparable level of AT2 cell surfactant markers (compared against hiPSC-derived AT2 cells as positive control) and a significant amount of AT1, as determined using the marker AQP5.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: ALOs contain basal cells, ciliated cells, and club cells.
source: ALOs also contained basal cells (as determined by the marker ITGA6, p75/NGFR, TP63), ciliated cells (as determined by the marker FOXJ1), and club cells (as determined by the marker SCGB1A1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Primary normal human bronchial epithelial cells (NHBE) had significantly higher expression of basal cell markers than the ALO lines.
source: As expected, the primary normal human bronchial epithelial cells (NHBE) had significantly higher expression of basal cell markers than the ALO lines (hence, served as a positive control), but they lacked stemness and club cells (hence, served as a negative control).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: NHBE cells lacked stemness and club cells.
source: As expected, the primary normal human bronchial epithelial cells (NHBE) had significantly higher expression of basal cell markers than the ALO lines (hence, served as a positive control), but they lacked stemness and club cells (hence, served as a negative control).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: ALO lines showed mixed cellularity with both proximal (basal-KRT5) and distal (AT1/AT2 markers) cell types within the same ALO line.
source: Such staining not only confirmed the presence of more than one cell type (i.e., mixed cellularity) of proximal (basal-KRT5) and distal (AT1/AT2 markers) within the same ALO line, but also, in some instances, demonstrated the presence of mixed cellularity within the same 3D structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: AT2 and basal cells were found in the same 3D organoid structure.
source: For example, AT2 and basal cells, marked by SFTPB and KRT5, respectively, were found in the same 3D structure (Figure 2J, interrupted curved lines).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Ciliated cells and goblet cells coexist within the same 3D organoid structure.
source: Similarly, ciliated cells and goblet cells stained by Ac-Tub and Muc5AC, respectively, were found to coexist within the same structure (Figure 2J, interrupted box; Figure 2K, arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: 3D organoid structures co-stained for CC10 and SFTPC were detected, indicative of mixed populations of club and AT2 cells.
source: Intriguingly, we also detected 3D structures that co-stained for CC10 and SFTPC (Figure 2J, bottom panel) indicative of mixed populations of club and AT2 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Each ALO line showed homotypic organoid structures that were relatively enriched in one cell type.
source: Besides the organoids with heterogeneous makeup, each ALO line also showed homotypic organoid structures that were relatively enriched in one cell type (Figure 2J, arrowheads pointing to two adjacent structures that are either KRT5- or SFTPB-positive).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The presence of mixed cellularity was documented in all three ALO lines.
source: Regardless of their homotypic or heterotypic cellular organization into 3D structures, the presence of mixed cellularity was documented in all three ALO lines (see multiple additional examples in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The coexistence of proximal and distal epithelial cells in lung organoids has been achieved in fetal lung bud tip-derived organoids by Lamers et al.
source: It is noteworthy that the coexistence of proximal and distal epithelial cells in lung organoids has been achieved in one another instance prior; Lamers et al. showed such mixed cellular composition in fetal lung bud tip-derived organoids Lamers et al., 2021.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Fetal lung bud tip-derived organoids by Lamers et al. lacked ciliated and goblet cells.
source: However, their model lacked ciliated and goblet cells (Lamers et al., 2021), something that we could readily detect in our 3D organoids.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: ALO models overall recapitulated the cell-type composition in the adult lung tissues from which they were derived.
source: using qRT-PCR of various cell-type markers as a measure, we confirmed that the ALO models overall recapitulated the cell-type composition in the adult lung tissues from which they were derived (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: ALO models retained their cell-type composition in later passages without significant notable changes in any particular cell type.
source: and retained such composition in later passages without significant notable changes in any particular cell type (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The mixed proximal and distal cellular composition of the ALO models and their degree of stability during in vitro culture was confirmed by flow cytometry.
source: The mixed proximal and distal cellular composition of the ALO models and their degree of stability during in vitro culture was also confirmed by flow cytometry (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: When 3D organoids were dissociated and plated as 2D monolayers on transwells, the AT2 signatures were virtually abolished with a concomitant and prominent emergence of AT1 signatures.
source: When 3D organoids were dissociated and plated as 2D monolayers on transwells, the AT2 signatures were virtually abolished with a concomitant and prominent emergence of AT1 signatures, suggesting that growth in 2D monolayers favors differentiation of AT2 cells into AT1 cells Shami and Evans, 2015 (Figure 3B, middle).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Growth in 2D monolayers favors differentiation of AT2 cells into AT1 cells.
source: When 3D organoids were dissociated and plated as 2D monolayers on transwells, the AT2 signatures were virtually abolished with a concomitant and prominent emergence of AT1 signatures, suggesting that growth in 2D monolayers favors differentiation of AT2 cells into AT1 cells Shami and Evans, 2015 (Figure 3B, middle).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: When organoids were grown in long-term 2D culture conditions in the ALI model, alveolar signatures were almost entirely replaced by a concomitant increase in ciliated and goblet cells.
source: The same organoids, when grown in long-term 2D culture conditions in the ALI model, showed a strikingly opposite pattern; alveolar signatures were almost entirely replaced by a concomitant increase in ciliated and goblet cells (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: ALI conditions favor growth as pseudo-stratified mucociliary epithelium.
source: These findings are consistent with the well-established notion that ALI conditions favor growth as pseudo-stratified mucociliary epithelium Prytherch et al., 2011; Dvorak et al., 2011.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: hiPSC-derived AT2 monolayers were enriched for AT2 and devoid of AT1 cells.
source: Because they were grown in the presence of CHIR99021 (an aminopyrimidine derivate that is a selective and potent Wnt agonist) Jacob et al., 2019; Yamamoto et al., 2017; Abdelwahab et al., 2019, which probably inhibits the AT2→AT1 differentiation, these monolayers were enriched for AT2 and devoid of AT1 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: CHIR99021 probably inhibits the AT2→AT1 differentiation.
source: Because they were grown in the presence of CHIR99021 (an aminopyrimidine derivate that is a selective and potent Wnt agonist) Jacob et al., 2019; Yamamoto et al., 2017; Abdelwahab et al., 2019, which probably inhibits the AT2→AT1 differentiation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: Submerged monolayers showed the prominent presence of both AT1 (AQP5-positive) and AT2 cells.
source: Submerged monolayers showed the prominent presence of both AT1 (AQP5-positive) and AT2 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: Compared to the 3D organoids, the 2D organoid cultures, especially the ALI model, showed a significant increase in ciliated structures.
source: Compared to the 3D organoids, the 2D organoid cultures, especially the ALI model, showed a significant increase in ciliated structures, as determined by acetylated tubulin (compare Ac Tub-stained panels in Figure 2J and K with Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The progressive prominence of ciliary structures from 3D to 2D models is in keeping with the fact that 3D ALOs represent the least differentiated state, whereas 2D submerged monolayers are intermediate and the 2D ALI monolayers are maximally differentiated.
source: The observed progressive prominence of ciliary structures from 3D to 2D models is in keeping with the fact that 3D ALOs that are yet to form lumen represent the least differentiated state, whereas 2D submerged monolayers are intermediate and the 2D ALI monolayers are maximally differentiated; differentiation is known to establish apicobasal polarity, which is essential for the emergence of mature cilia on the apical surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Differentiation establishes apicobasal polarity, which is essential for the emergence of mature cilia on the apical surface.
source: differentiation is known to establish apicobasal polarity, which is essential for the emergence of mature cilia on the apical surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge.

claim: The increase in ciliated epithelium in ALI models was associated with a concomitant decrease in KRT5-stained basal cells.
source: This increase in ciliated epithelium was associated with a concomitant decrease in KRT5-stained basal cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Loss of the basal cell marker KRT5 between submerged monolayers and the ALI model can be attributed to the expected conversion of basal cells to other cell types (i.e., ciliated cells).
source: Such loss of the basal cell marker KRT5 between submerged monolayers and the ALI model can be attributed to and the expected conversion of basal cells to other cell types (i.e., ciliated cells) Gras et al., 2017; Khelloufi et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: The integrity of the epithelial barrier formed by submerged monolayers derived from ALO was impaired by LPS challenge.
source: Compared to unchallenged controls, the integrity of the barrier was impaired by LPS, as indicated by a significant drop in the TEER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K and L)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: LPS has a disruptive role on the respiratory epithelium.
source: which is in keeping with the known disruptive role of LPS on the respiratory epithelium Kalsi et al., 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The short-term submerged monolayer favors distal differentiation (AT2→AT1).
source: the immunofluorescence images are in agreement with the RNA seq dataset; both demonstrate that the short-term submerged monolayer favors distal differentiation (AT2→AT1)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from multiple data types.

claim: The 21-day ALI model favors proximal mucociliary differentiation.
source: whereas the 21-day ALI model favors proximal mucociliary differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from multiple data types.

claim: Submerged ALO monolayers showed progressive changes during the 48–72 hr window after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Confocal imaging of infected ALO monolayers with anti-SARS-COV-2 nucleocapsid protein antibody showed that submerged ALO monolayers did indeed show progressive changes during the 48–72 hr window after infection (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: By 48 hpi, infected ALO monolayers showed the formation of 'reticulovesicular patterns' indicative of viral replication within modified host endoplasmic reticulum.
source: by 48 hpi, we observed the formation of 'reticulovesicular patterns' that are indicative of viral replication within modified host endoplasmic reticulum (Knoops et al., 2008; Figure 3G, left)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: By 72 hpi, infected ALO monolayers showed focal cytopathic effect (CPE) such as cell-rounding, detachment, and bursting of virions.
source: and by 72 hpi we observed focal cytopathic effect (CPE) (Kaye, 2006) such as cell-rounding, detachment, and bursting of virions (Figure 3G, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Ciliated airway cells are important for SARS-CoV-2 infectivity (i.e., viral entry, replication, and apical release).
source: Because multiple groups have shown the importance of the ciliated airway cells for infectivity (i.e., viral entry, replication, and apical release [Hou et al., 2020; Milewska et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020; Hui et al., 2020])
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: AT2 cells express high levels of viral entry receptors ACE2 and TMPRSS2.
source: AT2 cells, which express high levels of viral entry receptors ACE2 and TMPRSS2 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: AT2 cells are proficient in viral entry but are least amenable to sustained viral release and infectivity.
source: have been shown to be proficient in the viral entry but are least amenable to sustained viral release and infectivity (Hou et al., 2020; Hui et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: The 2D lung monolayers (both submerged and ALI models) were readily infected with SARS-CoV-2.
source: As expected, the 2D lung monolayers we generated, both the submerged and the ALI models, were readily infected with SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), as determined by the presence of the viral envelope gene (E gene; Figure 3H)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The kinetics of viral amplification differed between submerged and ALI monolayer models.
source: however, the kinetics of viral amplification differed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: The kinetics of the ALI monolayer model mirrored that of the primary airway epithelial monolayers.
source: When expressed as levels of E gene normalized to the peak values in each model (Figure 3H), the kinetics of the ALI monolayer model mirrored that of the primary airway epithelial monolayers; both showed slow beginning (0–48 hpi) followed by an exponential increase in E gene levels from 48 to 72 hpi.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The submerged monolayer model showed sustained viral infection during the 48–72 hpi window.
source: The submerged monolayer model showed sustained viral infection during the 48–72 hpi window (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, left).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The 48–72 hpi window was notably missing in monolayers of hiPSC-derived AT2 cells.
source: In the case of AT2 cells, the 48–72 hpi window was notably missing in monolayers of hiPSC-derived AT2 cells (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Proximal airway models (human bronchial airway epi [HBEpC]) showed high levels of sustained infectivity compared to distal models (human small airway epi [HSAEpC] and AT2) during the late phase (48–72 hpi window).
source: When we specifically analyzed the kinetics of viral E gene expression during the late phase (48–72 hpi window), we found that proximal airway models (human bronchial airway epi [HBEpC]) showed high levels of sustained infectivity than distal models (human small airway epi [HSAEpC] and AT2) to viral replication (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: ALO monolayers showed intermediate sustained infectivity (albeit with variability) during the late phase (48–72 hpi window).
source: the ALO monolayers showed intermediate sustained infectivity (albeit with variability).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claim: Both NHC (EIDD-parent) and its derivative pro-drug EIDD-2801 effectively reduced the viral titer in ALO monolayers in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Both compounds effectively reduced the viral titer in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3I), and the pro-drug derivative showed a better efficacy, as shown previously.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The pro-drug derivative EIDD-2801 showed better efficacy than NHC in reducing viral titer.
source: Both compounds effectively reduced the viral titer in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3I), and the pro-drug derivative showed a better efficacy, as shown previously.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Sustained viral infectivity is best simulated in monolayers that resemble the proximal mucociliary epithelium.
source: these findings show that sustained viral infectivity is best simulated in monolayers that resemble the proximal mucociliary epithelium, that is, 2D monolayers of lung organoids grown as ALI models and the primary airway epithelia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Proximal airway cells within the mixed-cellular ALO model appear to be sufficient to model viral infectivity in COVID-19.
source: Because prior studies conducted in patient-derived airway cells (Hou et al., 2020) mirror what we see in our monolayers, we conclude that proximal airway cells within our mixed-cellular model appear to be sufficient to model viral infectivity in COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion with a citation.

Despite mixed cellularity (proximal and distal), this fetal lung organoid model failed to induce the ViP signatures (Sahoo et al., 2021) (Figure 6H).

source: Second, among all the established lung models so far, ours features four key properties that are desirable whenever disease models are being considered for their use in HTP modes for rapid screening of candidate therapeutics and vaccines: (i) reproducibility, propagability, and scalability; (ii) cost-effectiveness; (iii) personalization; and (iv) modularity, with the potential to add other immune and nonimmune cell types to our multicellular complex lung model.

source: The ability to replicate donor phenotype and genotype in vitro allows for potential use as preclinical human models for phase '0' clinical trials.

evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as an acknowledgment of model limitations.

claim: The exact cellular proportion of ALOs was not assessed in this study.
source: While we successfully demonstrated the proximo-distal mixed cellular composition of the ALOs using four different approaches (flow cytometry, RNA seq, confocal immunofluorescence, and targeted qPCR) and showed that such mixed cellularity is preserved during prolonged culture, the exact cellular proportion was not assessed here.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as an acknowledgment of what was not done.

claim: The epithelial contributions to the host response in COVID-19 are important, but they alone cannot account for the response of the immune cells and the nonimmune stromal cells, and their crosstalk with the epithelium.
source: For instance, although the epithelial contributions to the host response are important, they alone cannot account for the response of the immune cells and the nonimmune stromal cells, and their crosstalk with the epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as an acknowledgment of model limitations.

claim: It is entirely possible that the epithelial signatures induced in infected ALO-derived monolayers are only a fraction of the actual epithelial response mounted in vivo.
source: Given that epithelial inflammation and damage is propagated by vicious forward-feedback loops of multicellular crosstalk, it is entirely possible that the epithelial signatures induced in infected ALO-derived monolayers are also only a fraction of the actual epithelial response mounted in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as speculation about model limitations.

claim: The ALO model already recapitulates approximately a quarter to half of the genes that are induced across diverse COVID-19-infected patient samples.
source: Regardless of the missing components, what appears to be the case is that we already have a model that recapitulates approximately a quarter to half of the genes that are induced across diverse COVID-19-infected patient samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as a summary of model performance.

claim: The ALO model can be further improved by the simultaneous addition of endothelial cells and immune cells to better understand the pathophysiological basis for DAD, microangiopathy, and organizing fibrosis in COVID-19.
source: This model can be further improved by the simultaneous addition of endothelial cells and immune cells to better understand the pathophysiological basis for DAD, microangiopathy, and even organizing fibrosis with loss of lung capacity that has been observed in many patients (Spagnolo et al., 2020); these insights should be valuable to fight some of the long-term sequelae of COVID-19.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as a future direction with a citation.

claim: Larger living biobanks of genotyped and phenotyped ALOs, representing donors of different age, ethnicity, predisposing conditions, and coexisting comorbidities, will advance understanding of why SARS-CoV-2 may trigger different disease course in different hosts.
source: Larger living biobanks of genotyped and phenotyped ALOs, representing donors of different age, ethnicity, predisposing conditions, and coexisting comorbidities, will advance our understanding of why SARS-CoV-2 and possibly other infectious agents may trigger different disease course in different hosts.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as a future direction.

claim: Proof-of-concept studies demonstrated the usefulness of the ALOs as human preclinical models for screening therapeutics in phase '0' trials, but optimization for HTP mode was not attempted.
source: Although we provide proof-of-concept studies in low-throughput mode demonstrating the usefulness of the ALOs as human preclinical models for screening therapeutics in phase '0' trials, optimization for the same to be adapted in HTP mode was not attempted here.
evidence: This is stated in the Limitations section as an acknowledgment of what was not done.
